description: 👥 We are a team of 2nd-year Software Engineering students from Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv (KNU). We have experience in web development, React, Next.js, TypeScript, JavaScript, Git/GitHub and AI tools. We are looking for motivated teammates with strong backend, AI/ML, data analysis, design, or product skills. We are open to new ideas and ready to build a strong project together. 🚀
summary:
Satellites have recorded active fires since 2000, but the record is split between two generations of sensors. VIIRS
(since 2012) sees several times more hotspots than MODIS (since 2000) for the same fires, so every long-term trend
shows a fake jump in 2012. Hotspot Harmony removes that jump. It rebuilds 25 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots as one record
in a single unit, MODIS-equivalent fire cell-days, and checks it on years the method never saw: the error is 5.8% per
month for Ukraine and 6.6% for Argentina, against more than 100% with no correction. On top of that record, a web app
lets anyone pick an area (a region, a country, or a polygon drawn on a 3D globe) and see its burning activity calendar
by day, month or any period, its unusual months, its peak burning months, and how far to trust each number. Fire
managers and researchers get a long-term answer to "is this season unusual here?" that does not depend on which
satellite was flying.
details:
What it does and how it works

1. A Python pipeline downloads the yearly FIRMS archives (MODIS Collection 6.1 on Terra and Aqua, VIIRS 375 m on

Suomi NPP and NOAA-20), brings them to one schema, keeps presumed vegetation fires and drops low-confidence

detections, and counts fire cell-days: a 1 km cell with at least one hotspot on a local solar day. Counting days a

cell burned, not single detections, already removes most of the difference in pixel size between the sensors.

2. Harmonization: for the VIIRS era each fire cell-day is weighted to what MODIS would have reported, from the years

both sensors flew together (2012-2021). Five methods were tried per country (a table by fire power, gradient

boosting, a context model and their means); the one with the lowest error on held-out years is kept. Up to 2021 the

record is MODIS as reported; from 2022 it is VIIRS NOAA-20 harmonized to MODIS, since MODIS is ending and Suomi NPP

stopped on 2 November 2026.

3. Validation: each year of 2012-2021 is hidden in turn, the method is fitted on the others and scored on the hidden

one. Ukraine: 2.7% per year and 5.8% per month; Argentina: 4.8% and 6.6%. The sensor jump in Ukraine (mean yearly

burning 2012-2016 over 2007-2011) is 2.00x in the raw record and 0.90x harmonized. The same check runs for 128

countries holding 99.8% of the world's fire cell-days.

4. A FastAPI service (DuckDB over Parquet) serves the record; a React + TypeScript web app shows it.

What the user gets

- A 3D globe (or a flat map) with the hotspots of any day, minute by minute, or of a month or any period, played day

by day.

- An area of interest picked as a region, a country (double-click on the globe) or a polygon drawn by click.

- For that area: a month-by-year burning activity calendar, the season against its history, unusual months (robust

z-score, kept only when beyond the method's error), peak burning months (the critical periods), where in the area it

burns most, and how burning changed between the two halves of the period on a map.

- "How far to trust this": the held-out error next to two baselines, so a user can judge every figure.

- Downloads: calendar data as CSV (with the area as WKT), hotspots as CSV, every chart as PNG. Shareable links.

- English and Ukrainian.


Benefits and expected impact

Long-term fire statistics stop changing with the satellite. A fire manager can ask whether this season is unusual for their district and get an answer that compares 2005 with 2025 on one scale; researchers get a consistent 25-year series and the code to rebuild it for any country.

Tools and languages

Python 3.12 (uv, DuckDB, pandas, scikit-learn, Shapely, FastAPI), TypeScript (React 19, Vite, MapLibre GL JS), Docker on Render for the API, Cloudflare Workers for the web app, GitHub Actions for tests and deploys. Charts are hand-written SVG.

Creativity

Instead of scaling hotspot counts by one factor, the record counts fire cell-days and weights each VIIRS cell-day to a MODIS equivalent, and the method is chosen by held-out error per country. Every number on the page comes with its measured error.

Factors considered

Scientific validity (every quoted number is reproducible with one command from the repository; tests on hand-worked fixtures); honesty about limits (a missing hotspot is not proof of no fire; days a sensor was down are marked as missing data; areas finer than the validated scale say so); accessibility (every chart has a table view and reads with the keyboard); a free host; credit for every data source.

Use of AI

An AI coding assistant (Claude Code by Anthropic) wrote most of the code, tests and documentation under the team's direction and review, reviewed pull requests, and recorded and captioned the demo video (the video carries a visible "AI-assisted" label). No language model runs inside the product; the harmonization fits its own small statistical and machine-learning models (scikit-learn) to the FIRMS data. Details: the "Use of AI tools" section of the README.
